cues.text: Let us turn now to the sixth topic in this study session: digital leadership and cultural transformation.
We have spent time on technologies, strategy and processes.
But technology alone never transforms an organisation.
People decide how technology is used, and the people who set direction are its leaders.
So we need to ask: what does leadership look like when an organisation is going through digital change, and what kind of culture must grow around it?
Let us begin with a definition.
Digital leadership is the guidance of an organisation through technological and business change.
It does three things.
First, it guides the organisation through that change.
Second, it aligns digital capabilities with the organisation's objectives, so that technology is never adopted for its own sake.
Third, it enables people to adapt, because tools only create value when people can use them well.
The source lists nine responsibilities, and I will take them in order.
One: vision, meaning a clear picture of where the organisation is heading digitally.
Two: strategic alignment, linking digital efforts to the wider business strategy.
Three: innovation, encouraging new products, services and ways of working.
Four: resource allocation, deciding where money, people and time are invested.
Five: collaboration, getting different groups to work together.
Six: governance, setting the rules, roles and accountability under which digital work happens.
Seven: customer value, keeping the focus on what customers actually gain.
Eight: skill development, building the abilities people need.
Nine: measurement, tracking whether the efforts are working.
Now let us look at styles of leadership, beginning with transformational leadership.
Transformational leadership inspires a shared vision, motivates people beyond their own self-interest, and supports their growth.
The source describes four commonly cited components.
The first is idealised influence.
This is role modelling: the leader behaves in ways that others respect and want to follow.
If a leader asks a team to use data but never does so personally, the message is weak.
The second is inspirational motivation.
This is vision: the leader articulates an appealing picture of the future that gives work meaning.
The third is intellectual stimulation.
Here the leader encourages people to challenge assumptions and to learn.
Questions like "why do we do it this way?" are welcomed rather than punished.
The fourth is individualised consideration.
This means coaching individuals, recognising that each person has different needs, strengths and development paths.
Set against this is transactional leadership.
It works through agreed rewards, clear expectations and corrective action when performance falls short.
For example, a target is set, a bonus is attached, and deviations are corrected.
The source says this is useful for stable execution, where the work is well understood and must be done reliably.
But it is insufficient on its own for transformational learning, because learning something new, and changing how an organisation works, needs more than rewards and corrections.
It needs vision, curiosity and growth.
Next, the source offers several further approaches.
I will name each one and explain it.
Adaptive leadership mobilises people to address complex challenges that have no ready-made solutions.
When nobody already knows the answer, the leader cannot simply issue instructions.
Instead, the leader gets people involved in working the problem out.
Situational leadership adjusts the direction and the support given according to context and capability.
A newcomer to a digital tool may need clear direction, while an experienced specialist may need more freedom and encouragement.
The leader changes approach accordingly.
Sociotechnical systems theory emphasises joint optimisation of technology, work and people.
The key word is joint.
You do not perfect the technology and then force people to fit it, nor the reverse.
You design technology, the way work is organised and the needs of people together, so that they fit one another.
Distributed, or shared, leadership empowers experts and teams within clear accountability.
Leadership is not held only at the top.
People with relevant expertise lead in their areas, but responsibility remains clear.
Servant leadership prioritises enabling others.
The leader sees the role as removing obstacles and equipping people to succeed.
The source adds an important point: these approaches can complement formal governance.
They do not replace rules, roles and accountability; they work alongside them.
Now to the traits and skills.

The source lists: visionary thinking, digital literacy, adaptability, empathy, communication, data literacy, ethical judgment, customer orientation, collaboration, systems thinking, experimentation and risk management.
That is twelve items.
Notice the mix of technical qualities, such as digital and data literacy, and human qualities, such as empathy, communication and ethical judgment.
An important qualification follows.
A digital leader need not be the best programmer.
What the leader must do is understand the implications of technology well enough to guide decisions and to ask informed questions.
So the aim is not to out-code the specialists, but to understand enough to lead them wisely.
Finally, the cultural shifts.
The source describes six movements, each from an old pattern to a new one.
First, from siloed departments to cross-functional teams.
Rather than each department working alone, people with different skills work together on shared goals.
Second, from rigid approval queues to delegated, accountable decisions.
Instead of every decision waiting for a senior sign-off, decisions are pushed to the people closest to the work, who remain accountable for them.
Third, from manual routines to appropriate automation.
Note the word appropriate: automate where it makes sense, not everything.
Fourth, from intuition-only decisions to evidence-informed decisions.
Experience and judgement still matter, but they are supported by data and evidence rather than relied upon alone.
Fifth, from fear of failure to bounded experiments.
People try new ideas within agreed limits, so that a failure is small and teaches something, rather than being feared.
Sixth, from one-time training to continuous learning.
Skills are developed constantly, not in a single course.
The section closes with a warning that is easy to overlook.
Build trust and inclusive access rather than imposing technology blindly.
If people are not trusted, or if some are left out of access to the tools and learning, then even excellent technology will meet resistance or fail to deliver.
Culture changes through trust and inclusion, not through instruction alone.
To bring it together: digital leadership is about vision, alignment and enabling people.
Leadership styles such as transformational, adaptive, situational, distributed and servant can complement governance.
The right traits combine technical understanding with human skills.
And the culture must move from silos, queues and fear toward collaboration, accountable delegation, evidence, experimentation and continuous learning, all built on trust and inclusion.
